opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, it comes down to the observation that so much of human progress has come from a process that is fundamentally open-ended. Science isn't about solving one fixed problem. It's about continually generating new questions, new hypotheses, new experiments, and then building on whatever you discover to go somewhere you couldn't have anticipated before. If we can build AI systems that take part in that loop more autonomously, rather than just being very good tools that we point at a well-defined benchmark, that could accelerate progress in a way that's qualitatively different from what we've seen so far.

A lot of my research has been on open-endedness: systems that keep producing artifacts that are both novel and learnable for an observer. Scientific discovery is maybe the most compelling instance of that. A good scientist isn't just optimizing an objective. They have a sense of what's interesting, of what's surprising given what we already know, and of what's likely to lead to further insight. Getting AI systems to have something like that sense of interestingness is a deep research problem in its own right, and I think it's one of the missing pieces on the path to more general intelligence.

What makes this moment exciting is that foundation models now give us a source of something like human notions of interestingness and a lot of prior knowledge about the world. You can combine that with search, self-improvement, and the ability to actually run experiments, whether in code, in simulation, or eventually in the lab. That's very different from a few years ago, when open-ended systems were confined to toy domains.

There's also a more personal motivation. The bottleneck in science is often the sheer number of ideas you can explore and the time it takes to test them. If AI systems can take on more of that exploratory work, propose hypotheses, check them, and surface the genuinely surprising results, then human researchers can spend more time on the parts that most need human judgment. Of course, that raises real questions about verification, safety, and making sure what these systems produce is actually correct and useful. But I think those are exactly the right problems to be working on.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AI-driven scientific discovery, search, and self-improvement, but does not state that applying discovery to AI itself could improve AI’s own improvement process.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most exciting questions you can ask right now. If you look at the history of science, progress has always been bottlenecked by the number of people who can do it, how fast they can run experiments, and how well they can communicate with each other. And for most of history, that's been a fairly small number of humans working with limited time and limited bandwidth.

What gets me excited about autonomous or semi-autonomous discovery is the idea that we could start to remove some of those bottlenecks. Imagine a system that can propose a hypothesis, design an experiment to test it, run that experiment, look at the results, and then refine its idea, all in a loop, and do that at a scale and speed that no human lab could match. That's a very different kind of accelerant than just having a better search engine or a better autocomplete.

The other reason I find it interesting is more personal, coming from my background in open-endedness. A lot of my work has been about systems that keep generating their own challenges and keep learning from them, rather than optimizing toward one fixed goal. Science is really the ultimate open-ended process. There's no single objective. You discover something, and that discovery opens up ten new questions you couldn't have even asked before. So in a sense, scientific discovery is the perfect domain for testing whether we can build systems that are genuinely open-ended rather than just good at a narrow task.

And then there's the honest point that we're not there yet. Current systems are good at remixing what's already known. The hard part, and the interesting part, is whether they can produce something genuinely novel and useful, something that surprises the experts in the field. That's a real scientific question about AI itself, and I find that extremely motivating.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous scientific discovery could be tested as a scientific question about AI itself, but does not state that this could let AI improve its own process of improvement.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility that AI could help us discover things we wouldn’t have thought to look for. There’s a difference between a system that answers a question we already know how to ask and one that can formulate a useful question, propose a hypothesis, and work out how to test it.

Science has this wonderful open-ended quality: you learn something, and that opens up new questions. If we can build systems that participate in that process, they could expand our ability to explore problems where our time and intuition are limiting factors.

Of course, generating an interesting idea isn’t enough. You need experiments, evidence, and ways to check whether it’s actually true. But the prospect of AI contributing to that whole cycle—of helping us build new knowledge—is what I find really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI helping with scientific discovery in general, but does not say that applying discovery to AI itself could improve AI’s own improvement process.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility that AI could help us discover things that we wouldn’t have thought to look for ourselves. There’s a difference between a system that answers a question we already know how to ask and one that can come up with an interesting hypothesis, design an experiment, and learn from the result.

Science involves this continual interaction with the world: you have an idea, you test it, and often you find out that your intuition was wrong. If we can build systems that participate in that process more autonomously, we might be able to explore a much larger space of ideas. And some of those ideas could help us make progress on problems that are very difficult for humans to solve today.

I also find it interesting as a question about intelligence. Can a system go beyond reproducing what people have already discovered and actually produce new knowledge? That seems like a very exciting capability to work toward.
